newsitem.title: FINLAND: Shipyard pact possible without U.S. - Bangemann.
newsitem.headline: Shipyard pact possible without U.S. - Bangemann.

text.p: An OECD accord to abolish subsidies to the shipbuilding industry could go forward without the United States if the European Union, Korea and Japan are aboard, European Union Commissioner Martin Bangemann said on Friday.

"If the the Koreans and Japanese accept (the idea of implementing the OECD accord without the U.S.), we could ratify the consensus only among Japan, Korea and the European Union," the Industry Commissioner told a news conference.
The United States is the only signatory to not yet have ratified the deal, sponsored by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development in 1994.
European Union shipowners have recently warned that a U.S. failure to ratify the accord could spark a race for subsidies which may hit freight markets.

But Bangemann said the competitive situation would actually allow other states who have ratified the OECD accord to move ahead on it without the United States -- what was not clear was if it would gain political support.

"It would even make sense because in fact the Americans are not a big competitor," he said, adding that the Americans' reservations on ratification stemmed from a law preserving a portion of shipbuilding for U.S. shipyards.
Bangemann said he did not know if political support could be mustered for Europe and its Asian partners to go it alone: "We have not discussed that. We will discuss it in the Council of Ministers."
If a three-way accord with Korea and Japan failed, Bangemann said the EU would need to devise its own system.

It was not possible to start negotiations afresh on an entirely new agreement, he said: Europe had already waited over two years for ratification of the existing one and twice postponed reforming a directive on the shipbuilding industry.
"We have already prolonged two times our ... shipbuilding directive ... and we cannot do that again," he said.
The EU's "own system" could, like the OECD accord, involve abolishing state subsidies to the shipbuilding industry, Bangemann said, but did not elaborate.
He added that he had discussed chances for American ratification of the OECD shipbuilding accord with U.S. officials on Tuesday, and Congressional ratification was unlikely.
"The U.S. administration is doing its best ... but you get the feeling that ratification will not be possible -- at least not of the text as it was signed," he said.

He said a precedent for moving ahead without the U.S. could be found in a 1995 accord on the liberalisation of cross-border financial services, which was brokered by the EU within the framework of the GATT/World Trade Organisation (WTO).

Bangemann was in Finland to discuss establishing a maritime technology database under a regional cooperation initiative, and for informal talks with Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen on issues including Baltic Sea cooperation and European Union enlargement.
